rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about which design axes (modality, encoder, profile, aggregation, fusion) matter or what performance floor to expect. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the most minimal configuration in the space—it uses the simplest RNA encoder (PCA), a single profile (no aggregation needed), and no image or fusion. It establishes the absolute performance baseline and calibrates how much headroom more complex choices (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, multimodal fusion) can provide. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With no prior data, the highest-value action is to anchor the search with the simplest interpretable reference. Any subsequent improvement (e.g., swapping PCA for scGPT, adding multiprofile aggregation, or introducing an image modality) can then be attributed to a specific design change rather than confounded with baseline difficulty. Starting with a complex multimodal config would make it impossible to decompose where gains or losses originate. A clean, minimal baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment under a limited budget.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, PCA-2000, singleprofile → 48.5% acc). The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality contributes any signal at all, which determines whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50) is the cleanest possible comparison: it matches config_001 in profile setting (singleprofile) and uses a standard, simple encoder (ResNet50 analogous to PCA), isolating the modality effect with no confounds from aggregation, fusion, or learned RNA encoders. If image performs comparably or better than RNA, it justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion and more complex image encoders. If it performs much worse, we can focus budget on RNA-side improvements (better encoders, multiprofile). This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis (modality) before committing to more complex configurations.

With only two completed experiments, evidence is very sparse. RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 0.485 acc clearly outperforms image (resnet50, singleprofile) at 0.208 acc, making RNA the dominant modality and its representation the most critical design choice to understand. Config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001: only the RNA encoder changes (pca_n2000 → scvi_n200), while profile setting, modality, and all other settings remain identical. This isolates whether a learned generative representation (scVI) can outperform a linear PCA projection, directly informing whether we should invest in more sophisticated encoders for all downstream multimodal experiments. Under a tight budget, resolving whether the RNA representation is the bottleneck before adding complexity (multiprofile, aggregation, fusion) is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485) in singleprofile RNA-only, and image-only (resnet50) is weak (0.208), suggesting RNA is the primary signal. Key uncertainty: whether multiprofile aggregation provides meaningful gains over singleprofile, which is a major structural axis affecting ~40 of the 51 configurations. This experiment (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool) tests that question using the best-known RNA encoder and the simplest aggregation, isolating the profile/aggregation effect with a single logical change from config_004. If multiprofile helps, it justifies investing in transformer aggregation and multimodal multiprofile variants; if it does not, it prunes a large portion of the search space. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice given the sparse 3-experiment history.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a large jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_004 (0.520/0.498), confirming that multiprofile + aggregation is the strongest direction. RNA encoders (scvi_n200 > pca_n2000) clearly dominate image-only (0.208). Uncertainty: We have only tested avgpool aggregation; whether transformer aggregation further improves or degrades performance is unknown, and this choice will propagate into every future multimodal experiment. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when paired with the best-known encoder (scvi_n200) and profile setting (multiprofile)? Why this experiment: config_006 changes exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool → transformer) relative to the current best result, giving a clean isolated comparison. The answer directly determines the aggregation design for all subsequent multimodal configurations, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile (avgpool) achieves 0.650 vs 0.520 for singleprofile — a ~13-point jump — while pca_n2000 singleprofile only reaches 0.485. Aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer) is nearly irrelevant (0.650 vs 0.653). The key uncertainty is whether the multiprofile benefit is a general property of having multiple profiles per cell or is specific to scvi_n200's learned latent representation. Question: Does pca_n2000 also gain substantially from multiprofile? config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable change from config_001 (pca_n2000, singleprofile), isolating the multiprofile effect for this encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly tests whether multiprofile is a broadly applicable design principle or an encoder-specific interaction, which determines whether we should prioritize exploring multiprofile with other encoders (scgpt) or focus on optimizing the scvi_n200 + multiprofile pipeline (e.g., via multimodal fusion). This one experiment reduces the most uncertainty about the dominant design axis identified so far.

Evidence: scvi_n200 consistently outperforms pca_n2000 (0.650 vs 0.591 in multiprofile+avgpool), and transformer vs avgpool yields a negligible difference (0.653 vs 0.650). The encoder choice is the dominant RNA-side design decision, yet scgpt has not been tested. Question: config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares scgpt vs scvi_n200 while holding profile setting and aggregation fixed, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next: The encoder axis shows the largest known variance (~6 pts) compared to aggregation (~0.3 pts), so resolving whether scgpt can match or beat scvi_n200 reduces the most important uncertainty. A favorable scgpt result would redirect the multimodal search; a negative result confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA representation and lets us focus remaining budget on fusion/multimodal questions with confidence.

Evidence: The current best model (config_006, rna_only/multiprofile/scvi_n200/transformer) achieves 0.653 acc, while image-only with resnet50 (config_010) is at 0.208—essentially random. This creates a critical uncertainty: is the image modality fundamentally uninformative for this task, or is resnet50 simply too weak an encoder to extract useful features? Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010, swapping only the image encoder to a much stronger pretrained ViT-L. It directly tests whether the image modality carries any predictive signal with a capable encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing in any of the 24+ multimodal fusion configurations, I need to know whether image features can contribute meaningfully at all. If ViT-L image-only remains near-random, multimodal fusion is unlikely to help and I should focus remaining budget on RNA-only refinements. If it shows a meaningful signal (e.g., >0.40), then multimodal experiments become well-justified and I can prioritize them. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty in the search space and guides all subsequent decisions.

1) Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the clear best performer (config_005/006: ~0.65 acc), while image-only is very weak (resnet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227). We have no data on whether combining modalities helps or hurts. 2) This experiment tests whether adding resnet50 image features via simple concat fusion to the best RNA configuration (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) yields any benefit over the RNA-only baseline (config_005, 0.650). It keeps aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) minimal to isolate the effect of image addition. 3) Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step: a positive result justifies investing in the 20+ remaining multimodal configs, while a negative or neutral result saves budget by confirming RNA-only is the right focus. It directly compares to config_005, changing only the addition of the image branch and concat fusion, making the causal interpretation clean.

Evidence: The best RNA-only model (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer, config_006) achieves 0.653 acc, while the only multimodal experiment (config_030: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat) achieves only 0.632 acc—worse than RNA-only. Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23 acc). This suggests either the image features are pure noise or the concat fusion is diluting the strong RNA signal. Question tested: config_031 changes only the fusion strategy (concat → weighted) relative to config_030, isolating whether a weighted combination can preserve the RNA signal while leveraging any residual image information. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison that directly answers whether multimodal fusion is viable with the current image encoder. If weighted fusion recovers performance to ~0.65+, it validates pursuing multimodal with better encoders; if it remains below RNA-only, it strongly indicates resnet50 image features are not contributing useful signal, redirecting budget toward either a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) or consolidating effort on the RNA-only pipeline.
